narrative:
The model determined that you have a 93% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for predicted success, this probability led directly to the rejection of your application.

The three factors that weighed most heavily in this decision were your academic performance in your third year of law school, your LSAT score, and your first-year academic performance. All three pushed the prediction strongly toward failure.

Your third-year class ranking was the single biggest reason for the negative outcome. Placing in the second decile, far below the average of roughly sixth decile among accepted students, signaled to the model that you struggled to keep pace with your peers later in the program. Your LSAT score of 28 was also substantially lower than the 37-point average of admitted students, giving the model further reason to expect difficulty passing the bar. Finally, your first-year ranking in the second decile, compared with an average around the sixth decile for accepted applicants, reinforced the pattern of academic challenge.

Taken together, these academic signals created a clear picture that the model interpreted as a very high risk of bar exam failure. 

What you should do next is focus on strengthening the areas the model flagged. Consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score, seeking targeted academic support or tutoring to improve your class standing, and then reapplying once you have demonstrated clearer progress. Many students improve these exact factors and gain admission on a later attempt.
